note: Prediction artefacts are NOT committed: they exceed Q5.4's size budget by two orders of magnitude and would break invariant 3 (no large binaries in git). ebnerd_baseline_submission.zip.archive_note: The prediction sits at the archive ROOT, matching the organisers' zip_submission_file (arcname=path.name). MIND's competition wants the same bare-filename layout, but that was established separately against its live scorer -- the two agree as a measured fact, not by derivation.
ebnerd_baseline_submission.zip.beyond_accuracy_note: All 200,000 beyond-accuracy rows carry impression_id=0. Verified in the written file with `grep -c '^0 '` = 200000: any group-by or de-duplicate on impression_id would have collapsed them to a single line and silently dropped the subset the competition built to measure diversity and novelty.
ebnerd_baseline_submission.zip.leaderboard_note: Accepted, which is what this submission was for: the archive layout and line format are confirmed against the live scorer, not inferred from the organisers' tooling. AUC 0.4305 is materially BELOW chance, and that is informative rather than a defect: EB-NeRD article ids increase with publication time, so ranking by article_id ascending puts the OLDEST articles first. Doing so is reliably worse than random, which independently confirms the freshness effect Q3.6 measured. The two baselines bracket chance -- MIND 0.5187, EB-NeRD 0.4305 -- so 'beats the baseline' is a different bar on each competition.
ebnerd_baseline_submission.zip.method_note: Candidates ranked by article_id ascending. Deterministic, no seed, and carrying no click signal -- expected to score near chance. Exists to prove 2469 accepts the file before the encoding run (OQ-6), exactly as the MIND baseline did.
ebnerd_baseline_submission.zip.superseded_note: Kept because it is the artefact Codabench actually scored (0.4305). The semantic submission now occupies predictions.zip; this file is byte-identical to what was uploaded, so the recorded score stays checkable against an artefact rather than resting on a number in a manifest.
ebnerd_baseline_submission.zip.validated_by: newsrec.submit.format.validate_file (Q5.3, streamed over 13.5M rows) and validate_archive (zip layout and member line count)

mind_baseline_submission.zip.archive_note: The zip holds a bare prediction.txt at its root. Codabench extracts a submission into its own res/ directory, so the scorer's '/app/input/res/prediction.txt' is the extraction destination, NOT a path the archive must contain -- a zip containing res/prediction.txt lands at res/res/prediction.txt and is rejected with the identical error. Settled against the live scorer after two rejections; EB-NeRD (2469) uses the same bare-filename layout per the organisers' zip_submission_file.
mind_baseline_submission.zip.leaderboard_note: Accepted, which is what this submission was for: the archive layout and line format are now confirmed against the live scorer rather than inferred. The score itself is the floor a real retriever must beat, not a result. Alphabetical article_id ordering carries no click signal, but MIND ids are assigned roughly in creation order, so the ordering has a faint recency component -- which is why chance here reads as 0.519 rather than 0.500.
mind_baseline_submission.zip.method_note: Candidates ranked by article_id ascending. Deterministic and carries no information about clicks -- expected to score near random. Its purpose is to prove the file format is accepted before the full pipeline runs (OQ-6).
mind_baseline_submission.zip.superseded_note: Kept because it is the artefact Codabench actually scored (0.5187). The hybrid now occupies mind_submission.zip; this file is byte-identical to what was uploaded, so the recorded score stays checkable rather than resting on a number in a manifest.
mind_baseline_submission.zip.validated_by: newsrec.submit.format.validate_file (Q5.3, line format and coverage) and validate_archive (zip layout and member line count)

mind_submission.zip.cold_row_note: 29,108 rows (1.23%) have no history, so both signals are silent and the ranking falls through to article_id — identical to the accepted baseline. Verified against it: on lists of 5+ candidates the hybrid differs on 98.7% of rows; shorter lists agree more often purely by chance (2-candidate lists have only two possible orderings).
mind_submission.zip.leaderboard_note: AUC 0.6114 against the article_id baseline's 0.5187 on the same file format, +0.0927. Offline, this configuration measured 0.6067 on mind_small's test split; the leaderboard returned 0.6114 on MINDlarge_test -- a gap of 0.0047 between a prediction made on one corpus and a result on another, larger one. That is closer than the two corpora's differences warrant assuming in advance, so it is recorded as encouraging rather than as evidence the offline harness is calibrated to four decimal places.
mind_submission.zip.method_note: 0.30 * minmax(bm25) + 0.70 * minmax(cosine), normalised per impression. Alpha was chosen on the VALIDATION split by eval/hybrid.py::select_on_val, never on a split any number is reported from, and kept an established gain on test: AUC 0.6067 vs 0.5985 semantic-only, delta +0.0082 [+0.0027,+0.0136]. Both EB-NeRD corpora independently selected alpha=0 on val, so EB-NeRD is submitted semantic-only.
mind_submission.zip.tie_break: (score, article_id). MINDlarge_test has no labels, so the offline training-period popularity tie-break (q2_plan D8) cannot be computed and is not invented. Cold rows therefore rank exactly like the article_id baseline.

predictions.zip.coverage_note: BOTH halves are checked. The first run had candidate coverage 1.0000 and ZERO user vectors — history ids are Int32 while the embedding table keys on str — which produced a valid, accepted file byte-identical to the baseline. MIN_USER_COVERAGE now refuses to write below 0.99.
predictions.zip.differs_from_baseline: 99.9% of the first 200,000 lines, and 99.9% on lists of 5+ candidates
predictions.zip.leaderboard_note: AUC 0.5508 against the article_id baseline's 0.4305 on the same file format, +0.1203. The offline harness predicted this submission's four ranking metrics on ebnerd_small's test split (n=2,000) before it was scored, and ALL FOUR leaderboard values fall inside the offline 95% bootstrap interval: AUC 0.5508 in [0.5357,0.5649], MRR 0.3510 in [0.3350,0.3613], nDCG@5 0.3916 in [0.3718,0.4017], nDCG@10 0.4679 in [0.4559,0.4805]. The AUC agrees to 3e-05, which is coincidence at that precision -- the interval is 0.029 wide -- and is not evidence of calibration to four decimal places. What the four hits do support is that a 2,000-row sample of a 244,647-row split predicted a 13,536,710-row test set from a later period. Full scorer output, including the per-day and beyond-accuracy blocks, in predictions/leaderboard_ebnerd_2469.json.
predictions.zip.method_note: Cosine between each user's pooled history vector and each candidate's article vector. NO lexical term: eval/hybrid.py swept the blend weight on the VALIDATION split and both EB-NeRD corpora independently selected alpha=0, their val curves falling monotonically from zero. MIND selected 0.30 and is submitted as a hybrid; the asymmetry is a measurement, not a preference.
predictions.zip.tie_break: (-score, article_id); cold users fall through to article_id order
predictions.zip.validated_by: newsrec.submit.format.validate_file (Q5.3, streamed over 13.5M rows) and validate_archive (zip layout and member line count)

mind_nrms_submission.zip.leaderboard_note: AUC 0.6290 against the article_id baseline's 0.5187 (+0.1103) and against A1's hybrid submission's 0.6114 (+0.0176) on the same file format. That gain is on AUC ONLY: the A1 hybrid remains slightly ahead on MRR (0.2969 vs 0.2905), nDCG@5 (0.3179 vs 0.3122) and nDCG@10 (0.3732 vs 0.3700). The offline harness predicted this submission's four ranking metrics on mind_small's test split (n=2,000) before it was scored: nDCG@5 (0.3122) and nDCG@10 (0.3700) fall INSIDE their offline 95% bootstrap intervals; AUC (0.6290) and MRR (0.2905) fall OUTSIDE (AUC above the upper bound, MRR below the lower bound) -- reported honestly rather than citing only the two that agree. A plausible, unverified reason: AUC/MRR are sensitive to where the clicked article sits among ALL candidates, while nDCG@5/@10 only look at the top of the ranking, so a difference in MINDlarge_test's candidate-list-length distribution versus mind_small's would move the first pair more than the second. Full scorer output and the CI comparison in predictions/leaderboard_mind_13967.json.
mind_nrms_submission.zip.method_note: A2 Q3's re-ranker, not Q2's feature-based MLP. Chosen over the literal best-val-nDCG@10 rule (which picks the MLP on MIND, 0.3692 vs NRMS's 0.3412 on validation nDCG@10, figures as of the final retrain) because the MLP's dominant feature, popularity_train, is non-zero for only 5.6% of MIND submission candidates -- measured on 20,000 lines of MINDlarge_test -- so it would score far outside the distribution it was fitted on. NRMS needs only an article embedding and a category label, both of which MINDlarge_test supplies in full; see OQ-14 for the full reasoning and submit/nrms_predict.py's module docstring.
mind_nrms_submission.zip.tie_break: argsort(-score, kind="stable"); MINDlarge_test has no labels, so the offline training-period popularity tie-break cannot be computed and is not invented -- ties fall through to the publisher's own candidate order.
mind_nrms_submission.zip.validated_by: newsrec.submit.format.write_lines + zip_prediction (Q5.3), plus tests/test_nrms_predict.py's row-count/permutation/positional-order checks

ebnerd_nrms_submission.zip.leaderboard_note: A2 Q5.5. Uploaded 2026-09; Codabench's own status for this submission reports elapsedTime, exitCode, ingestionElapsedTime and ingestionExitCode all null -- the job never started executing, which is a different failure mode from a format rejection (those return a non-null exit code with a validation message). Investigated and ruled out locally: every one of the 13,536,710 rows' candidate-list lengths matches ebnerd_testset's truth file exactly and in order (full comparison, not a sample); the zip is byte-valid (unzip -t: no errors); the submission is 219 MB against the competition's own documented reference-submission size of 220 MB, so it is not oversized; the competition's execution budget is 172,800 seconds (48h), which a never-started job cannot have exceeded. The competition runs on a legacy codalab-legacy:py39 Docker image with a 279.9 GB reference dataset that must be provisioned per job -- the leading hypothesis is a platform-side worker/provisioning failure, not a defect in this file. Not yet resolved as of this entry.
